title: Free attachment style test: secure, anxious or avoidant? — cv.cm
description: Free attachment style quiz for adults. Answer 16 statements about close relationships to see whether your style is secure, anxious, avoidant or fearful-avoidant. No sign-up.
lede: How do you act in close relationships? This quiz measures attachment anxiety and avoidance and places you in one of four styles.
about: Attachment theory began with John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth's studies of children and was extended to adult romantic relationships by Hazan and Shaver. Modern research measures two dimensions: anxiety (fear of rejection) and avoidance (discomfort with closeness).

Your style comes from where you fall on both: low on both is secure. This short quiz was written for cv.cm and is based on that two-dimension model. Styles can change with time and with supportive relationships.

faq.q: What are the four attachment styles?
faq.a: Secure (low anxiety, low avoidance), anxious (high anxiety), avoidant (high avoidance), and fearful-avoidant (high on both).
Yes. A long, stable relationship, therapy, and conscious practice can move people toward security, which researchers call earned security.

faq.q: Should I answer about my current partner?
faq.a: Answer about how you generally feel in close relationships, not only about one person.
Secure attachment is linked with the most relationship satisfaction, but every style makes sense as a response to past experience, and each can grow.

items: I worry that the people I love won't care about me as much as I care about them.
I prefer not to show others how I feel deep down.
I need a lot of reassurance that I'm loved.
I get uncomfortable when a partner wants to be very close.
When someone I love is away, I worry they'll lose interest in me.
I find it easy to depend on people I'm close to.
I get upset when my partner doesn't reply for a while.
I value my independence more than closeness.
I feel comfortable sharing private thoughts with my partner.
I rarely worry about being left.
I pull away when a relationship starts getting serious.
I often wish my partner's feelings for me were as strong as mine.

I overthink small changes in my partner's mood.
Turning to people I love for comfort helps me.

secure.name: Secure
secure.body: You are comfortable with closeness and with independence. You trust partners, say what you need, and handle conflict without panicking. Keep it up: your steadiness helps the people around you feel safe too.

anxious.name: Anxious (preoccupied)
anxious.body: You want closeness and worry about losing it, so you may seek reassurance or read a lot into small signals. Naming your needs directly, and soothing yourself before reacting, makes relationships feel calmer.

avoidant.name: Avoidant (dismissive)
avoidant.body: You value independence and feel uneasy when others get too close or depend on you. You may pull back when things get serious. Practising small steps of openness lets people support you without taking your freedom.

fearful.name: Fearful-avoidant (disorganized)
fearful.body: You want closeness but also fear it, so you may swing between reaching out and pulling away. This often comes from painful experiences. Patience, a steady partner, and support from a therapist can help a lot.
